description: Mountains are not permanent. They rise as continents collide, and they are worn down from the moment they appear.

body.heading: Continents in slow collision
paragraphs: When two continental plates converge, neither sinks easily — both are too buoyant. Instead, the crust crumples. Rock layers fold like a pushed tablecloth, crack along faults, and stack atop one another, thickening the crust and lifting a mountain range. The process is called orogeny.

The Himalayas are the living example: India continues to plough into Asia at a few centimetres a year, and the range rises by roughly a centimetre annually in places. Mount Everest's height has been re-measured repeatedly because it keeps, very slowly, changing.

body.heading: Uplift versus erosion
paragraphs: From the instant rock rises, wind, water, ice and gravity attack it. Rivers saw through ranges, glaciers quarry them, and landslides deliver whole hillsides to the valleys. Many old ranges, like the Appalachians, are the worn-down roots of mountains once far taller.

A mountain range is therefore a balance sheet: uplift deposits height, erosion withdraws it. The Alps, Andes and Himalayas are still gaining. The quiet, rounded hills of ancient ranges are what remain when the deposits stop.

takeaway: Mountains grow where plates collide and crust crumples, while erosion works to wear them down from the start.
